source_title: Limitations on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles — Law Enforcement Evidentiary and Warrant Restriction
revision_date: Amended 2019 (Ch. 178, L. 2019); no amendment identified since
uas_topic: Law enforcement UAS use; search-warrant/evidentiary limitation; privacy/surveillance
regulated_party: Law enforcement and any party seeking to introduce UAV-derived information in a Montana prosecution or proceeding
regulated_activity: Using information gathered from a UAV as evidence, or as the basis for a search-warrant probable-cause affidavit, in a Montana prosecution or proceeding
requirement_type: Evidentiary exclusion/admissibility restriction conditioned on a warrant or recognized exception
permit_or_approval_required: No (not a permit process; a warrant or judicially recognized exception is the qualifying condition for admissibility)
public_agency_only: No (governs admissibility of UAV-derived information generally in any prosecution or proceeding; principally constrains law-enforcement use of such information)
commercial_operator_relevance: Indirect — does not regulate a private commercial operator's flight operations, but governs whether UAV-derived information (including a private operator's own data later sought by law enforcement or a civil litigant) is admissible
aec_relevance: Indirect — relevant where an AEC firm's UAS-collected imagery or data could later be sought by law enforcement or introduced in litigation (e.g., accident documentation, dispute evidence); not itself a flight-operations restriction
summary: Mont. Code Ann. § 46-5-109 provides that in any prosecution or proceeding within Montana, information from an unmanned aerial vehicle is not admissible as evidence unless obtained (a) pursuant to a search warrant, (b) under a judicially recognized exception to the warrant requirement, or (c) during investigation of a motor-vehicle crash scene on or involving a public roadway. Subsection (2) separately bars use of UAV-obtained information in a probable-cause affidavit unless obtained under one of those same three circumstances. Subsection (3) defines "unmanned aerial vehicle" as an aircraft operated without direct human intervention from on or within the aircraft, expressly excluding satellites. Originally enacted in 2013 (Ch. 377) and amended in 2019 (Ch. 178) to add the motor-vehicle-crash exception.
verification_status: Fetched and read in full directly from mca.legmt.gov (official Montana Code Annotated, 2025 edition).
notes: One of Montana's earliest UAS-specific statutes (2013); establishes a warrant-based evidentiary framework rather than a flight-operations permit scheme. No further amendment since 2019 identified in this pass.

source_title: Criminal Trespass by Unmanned Aerial Vehicle -- Exceptions
effective_date: 2025 (Laws, 2025, ch. 410, SB 493); specific effective-date clause not independently confirmed in this pass
uas_topic: Trespass; privacy/surveillance; property rights over low-altitude airspace
regulated_party: Any person operating a UAV; property owners/residents as protected parties
regulated_activity: Knowingly causing a UAV to fly 200 feet or lower over the property or residence of another without authorization of the owner or resident
permit_or_approval_required: No (authorization from the property owner/resident is the qualifying condition, not a governmental permit; no application process specified)
public_agency_only: No -- applies broadly to any person, though subsection (3) exempts specified government, peace-officer, utility/broadband, easement, and FAA-licensed business-purpose operations
commercial_operator_relevance: Yes -- directly relevant to any commercial UAS operator flying at or below 200 feet AGL over property without the owner's or resident's authorization
aec_relevance: Yes -- directly relevant to AEC firms conducting low-altitude mapping, inspection, or construction-monitoring flights over Montana private property; the FAA-licensed 'legitimate business purposes' exception in (3)(e) and the utility/broadband infrastructure-inspection exception in (3)(d) are especially pertinent
summary: Mont. Code Ann. § 45-6-210, enacted in 2025 (Laws 2025, ch. 410, SB 493), makes it a criminal trespass for a person to knowingly cause a UAV to fly 200 feet or lower over the property or residence of another without the property owner's or resident's authorization; a violation is fined $500. Subsection (3) exempts: UAS operations by a federal, state, tribal, or local government unit/agency (including contractors) for public safety, firefighting, law enforcement, or emergency response; peace-officer operations conducted under § 46-5-109; operations within an easement with the dominant-tenement owner's permission; utility or broadband-service-provider operations to assess damage or inspect property/infrastructure (including cell towers and wireless infrastructure); and operations by an FAA-licensed owner/operator conducting legitimate business purposes consistent with FAA rules, licenses, and exemptions. 'Unmanned aerial vehicle' takes the meaning given in § 76-13-102.
verification_status: Fetched and read in full directly from mca.legmt.gov (official Montana Code Annotated, 2025 edition), including the cross-referenced definition pointer to § 76-13-102 and the exceptions in subsection (3).
notes: Newly enacted (2025) and already the subject of active legislative/legal debate: at a May 13, 2026 Environmental Quality Council hearing, Lt. Gov. Kristen Juras cited this statute to argue that drone-assisted verification of 'corner-crossing' constitutes airspace trespass (see printable summary Non-Regulatory Context). The statute's precise effective date (standard October 1, 2025 default vs. a special clause) was not independently confirmed in this pass.

source_title: Obstruction of Aerial Wildfire Suppression Activities; Related Local-Ordinance Preemption
revision_date: § 76-13-214 amended 2023 (Ch. 662, § 4, L. 2023); § 7-1-111 separately and frequently amended for unrelated subsections (most recently 2025, Ch. 537, § 2), with subsection (20) itself unchanged since 2017
binding_level: Binding (statute); criminal (misdemeanor) for § 76-13-214; binding limitation on local self-government ordinance power for § 7-1-111(20)
uas_topic: Wildfire-related UAS interference; state preemption of local UAS ordinances (wildfire-specific only)
regulated_party: Any person operating a UAV near active aerial wildfire suppression; local governments with self-government powers (as to ordinance authority)
regulated_activity: Obstructing, impeding, preventing, or otherwise interfering with lawful aerial wildfire suppression activities by any means, including UAV use; a local government enacting an ordinance governing private UAV use in relation to a wildfire
requirement_type: Prohibition (§ 76-13-214) plus express denial of local-government ordinance power on this specific subject (§ 7-1-111(20))
public_agency_only: No -- § 76-13-214 applies to any person (with an exception for government/contracted UAS operations for public-safety purposes); § 7-1-111(20) applies only to local self-governing units' ordinance-making power, not to private operators directly
commercial_operator_relevance: Yes -- a commercial UAS operator flying near active wildfire suppression is directly subject to § 76-13-214's prohibition and penalty
aec_relevance: Yes -- directly relevant to AEC/environmental-monitoring UAS missions conducted near active wildfires or fire-affected sites; also establishes that Montana's local governments cannot impose their own, potentially conflicting, wildfire-related UAS ordinances
summary: Mont. Code Ann. § 76-13-214 prohibits a person from obstructing, impeding, preventing, or otherwise interfering with lawful aerial wildfire suppression activities by any means, including by use of an unmanned aerial vehicle system; a violation is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $1,500, and the fine does not limit other remedies for property/person damage or recovery of wildfire suppression costs caused by the violation. Subsection (3)(a) exempts UAS operations conducted by a unit or agency of the federal, state, tribal, or local government (including contractors) for public safety and welfare purposes, including firefighting, law enforcement, or emergency response. Enacted concurrently in 2017 (HB 644) was a companion amendment to Montana's 'powers denied' statute for self-governing local units, now codified at § 7-1-111(20), which expressly bars a local government unit with self-government powers from enacting any ordinance governing the private use of a UAV in relation to a wildfire -- a narrow, subject-specific preemption rather than a general preemption of local UAS ordinances.
verification_status: Both § 76-13-214 and § 7-1-111 (including subsection (20)) were fetched and read in full directly from mca.legmt.gov (official Montana Code Annotated, 2025 edition); the Legislative Services Division's own 2019 bill-history primer on drones was cross-checked and corroborates that both provisions originated together in 2017 HB 644.
notes: PREEMPTION SCOPE NOTE: several secondary drone-law aggregator sites could be read to imply broader Montana preemption of local UAS ordinances. Verified primary text shows the preemption is narrow and single-subject: § 7-1-111(20) denies local self-government units only the power to regulate private UAV use 'in relation to a wildfire.' No broader statewide preemption of local UAS ordinances (e.g., covering launch/landing, park rules, or general operational ordinances) was located; local ordinances such as Missoula's park-drone restriction reportedly remain in effect (see printable summary Unresolved Operational Questions).

source_title: Unlawful Use of Aircraft (Hunting-Related Drone/UAV Restrictions)
citation: Mont. Code Ann. § 87-6-208 (2025); definition of "aircraft" at Mont. Code Ann. § 87-6-101(3) (2025)
binding_level: Binding (statute); criminal (misdemeanor) with hunting/fishing/trapping license and privilege forfeiture
uas_topic: Hunting-related UAS restriction (drone-assisted scouting, spotting, herding, and hunt interference)
regulated_party: Any person hunting, or using a UAV/aircraft in connection with hunting, in Montana
regulated_activity: Using an aircraft (statutorily defined to include unmanned aerial vehicles) to kill/take wildlife directly from the aircraft; to spot/locate a game animal for hunting purposes within 24 hours of using the aircraft; to concentrate, pursue, drive, rally, or stir up game/migratory birds/fur-bearing animals; to intentionally interfere with a hunt by disturbing animal behavior; to land in violation of land-use travel plans or without written permission on private property while pursuing game; or to spot/locate and communicate an animal's location to a hunter while airborne or within 24 hours after
requirement_type: Prohibition with limited exceptions (emergency, search and rescue, Department of Livestock predator control, agricultural-operation support)
commercial_operator_relevance: Yes -- directly restricts any commercial UAS operation (including a hired aerial-scouting or wildlife-survey flight) that spots/locates game, herds/pursues wildlife, or aids a hunt, whether or not the operator is the hunter
aec_relevance: Limited but material -- most directly relevant to environmental-monitoring, wildlife-survey, or land-management UAS missions conducted in areas and seasons where hunting occurs, since the same flight characteristics (spotting/tracking wildlife) that trigger this statute can arise in non-hunting environmental UAS work; not applicable to typical mapping/construction/infrastructure-inspection missions absent a hunting nexus
summary: Mont. Code Ann. § 87-6-208 prohibits using an aircraft -- statutorily defined at § 87-6-101(3) as 'any manned or unmanned aerial vehicle or device that is used or intended to be used for flight in the air,' expressly reaching drones/UAS -- to kill or take game from the aircraft; to spot or locate a game animal for hunting purposes within 24 hours of use; to concentrate, pursue, drive, rally, or stir up game birds, migratory birds, game animals, or fur-bearing animals; to intentionally interfere with a hunt, including by disturbing animal behavior; to land in violation of state/federal land-use travel plans or without written permission on private property while pursuing game; or to spot/locate an animal and communicate its location to a hunter while airborne or within 24 hours afterward. Exceptions apply for emergencies, search and rescue, Department of Livestock predator control, and support of an agricultural operation. Penalties range from a $300-$1,000 fine and up to 6 months' imprisonment for a general violation up to a $500-$2,000 fine, up to 6 months' imprisonment, and 30-month loss of hunting/fishing/trapping privileges for using an aircraft to kill/take specified big game.
verification_status: Both § 87-6-208 and the § 87-6-101 definitions section were fetched and read in full directly from mca.legmt.gov/archive.legmt.gov (official Montana Code Annotated, 2025 edition), confirming the 'aircraft' definition expressly includes unmanned aerial vehicles.
notes: This is a statutory (MCA) restriction, not an ARM/administrative rule as some secondary sources imply; the drone-assisted scouting/spotting/herding prohibition is directly codified in Title 87 (Fish and Wildlife). Repeated 2023 and 2025 amendments (most recently 2025 Ch. 553) indicate active, ongoing legislative attention to this statute; the exact substance of each individual amendment was not itemized in this pass beyond confirming the current consolidated text above.

source_title: Limitations on Excess Property Provided to Local Law Enforcement (Armored/Weaponized Drones)
uas_topic: State/local-government UAS procurement restriction (armored/weaponized drones via military-surplus programs); law-enforcement equipment militarization limits
regulated_party: Local-government law-enforcement agencies (as defined by reference to Title 7, chapter 32)
regulated_activity: Receiving armored or weaponized drones (or combat-configured/coded aircraft, grenades/explosives, silencers, or militarized armored vehicles) from a federal military-equipment surplus program
requirement_type: Prohibition (categorical bar on receiving specified military-surplus property) plus a funding-source restriction on any permitted military-surplus purchases
public_agency_only: Yes -- applies only to local-government law-enforcement agencies as purchasers/recipients, not to private AEC consultants
commercial_operator_relevance: No -- governs local law-enforcement agency acquisition, not private commercial UAS operation
aec_relevance: Indirect -- relevant primarily as background context for AEC firms partnering with or contracting to Montana local law-enforcement agencies on UAS-related equipment or services; not applicable to a private firm's own commercial fleet
summary: Mont. Code Ann. § 7-32-401(1)(a) bars a local-government law-enforcement agency from receiving drones that are armored, weaponized, or both, from a military-equipment surplus program operated by the federal government; the same subsection separately bars receipt of combat-configured/coded aircraft, grenades/explosives and launchers, silencers, and militarized armored vehicles. Subsection (2) requires that any property a law-enforcement agency does purchase from such a surplus program be paid for with state or local funds only, not federal funds. 'Law enforcement agency' is defined by cross-reference to the local-government law-enforcement services authorized under Title 7, chapter 32.
verification_status: Fetched and read in full directly from mca.legmt.gov (official Montana Code Annotated, 2025 edition), including confirmation of the enacting session-law citation (Ch. 261, L. 2015).
notes: A general web search initially returned only a secondary AI-generated summary describing this provision without directly quoting or citing the statute; the exact text and section number were independently confirmed by locating and fetching the primary source via the Title 7, Chapter 32, Part 4 table of contents. This restriction applies only to local-government law-enforcement agencies, not to the state itself, other state agencies, or private AEC consultants.

summary: Executive Order 11-2019 (Aug. 29, 2019) created the Montana Unmanned Aerial Systems Council, administratively attached to MDT, comprising representatives of DEQ, DNRC, FWP, MDT, Department of Livestock, Department of Justice, the Montana University System, and stakeholders. The order directed the Council to issue, by November 15, 2019 and January 1, 2020 respectively, draft and final statewide UAS procurement procedures (covering a cost-benefit analysis for purchases over $1,000 and related recording/reporting/disclosure requirements), and to issue, by April 1, 2020 and August 1, 2020 respectively, a draft and final 'Montana Unmanned Aerial Systems Plan' addressing centralized state-agency UAS oversight, operator training/certification standards, interagency coordination, and citizen-privacy considerations regarding state UAS use over private property. By its own terms, the order specifies the Council 'shall complete its work and cease to exist by September 1, 2020, unless rescinded or renewed by subsequent executive order.'

A targeted search for a renewal, rescission, or superseding executive order, and for the Council's final 'Montana Unmanned Aerial Systems Plan' deliverable, did not locate either; confidence is Moderate because the order's current (expired) status rests on the order's own sunset clause plus a negative search result for a renewal, rather than an affirmative rescission record.
